lesson_title: Bricks, Clicks and a Kitchen Scale: Chemistry Exam Essentials
hook_text: You can count 1 200 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 molecules with a kitchen scale. Chemists do it every day.
clip_script: Chemists have a counting problem: atoms are too small to count one by one, but reactions happen atom by atom. The solution is the oldest trick in any kitchen — count by weighing. If one egg weighs 60 grams, then 720 grams of eggs is 12 eggs. No counting happened; the scale did it. The mole is the chemist's dozen — just absurdly larger: 6,02 times 10 to the 23 particles. One mole of water weighs 18 grams. Put 36 grams of water on the scale and you KNOW, without counting, that you hold 2 moles: more than a trillion trillion molecules, counted by a kitchen scale.
visual_style: A kitchen scale piled with eggs morphing into a beaker of water; the readout flipping from grams to a ludicrously long particle count that scrolls off screen; the periodic table appearing as a price list.
mood: Delighted heist energy — an impossible counting job pulled off with the humblest tool in the house.
pacing: Fast egg-crate setup, the mole reveal as the punch, the 36-gram water payoff landing on the scrolling count.
